meta.title: Bright — practise medical emergencies with an AI
meta.description: Practise medical emergencies by typing what you'd actually do. The AI plays the patient or a doctor quizzing you, scores every answer, and shows you where you're weakest. Free, in your browser or on Android.
meta.ogAlt: Bright — a step for your brighter future

hero.eyebrow: Free · In your browser and on Android
hero.title: Practise the emergency before it's real.
hero.description: The AI plays the patient, or a doctor asking what you'd do next. You type the answer you'd actually give, and every answer comes back scored, with a line on what you got right and what you missed.
hero.note: Look around without an account. Sign in with Google for graded answers in the browser — no key needed.

result.slogan: A step for your brighter future

drill.title: One case, answered in your own words
drill.lede: No multiple choice. The case moves one focused question at a time, and each answer is graded before the next one comes.

steps.label: Pick the case
steps.title: Choose the emergency and your role
steps.body: Ten emergencies at three difficulty levels. You're the doctor, nurse or EMT; the AI is the patient, or a doctor quizzing you.

steps.label: Answer
steps.title: Type what you'd actually do
steps.body: Nothing to pick between. You have to come up with the assessment and the next step yourself, the way you would on the day.

steps.label: Get graded
steps.title: A score and a reason, every turn
steps.body: Each answer gets a mark out of ten and a sentence or two on what was right or missing. Ending the session gives you a short wrap-up.

progress.title: It remembers where you're weak
progress.lede: A chatbot forgets you after every conversation. Bright keeps score across sessions, so the fiftieth drill is aimed better than the first.

points.title: An average for every emergency
points.body: Every graded answer counts toward that case's average, so you can see which ones you're solid on and which you're guessing at.

points.title: Which way it's heading
points.body: Your last few sessions are compared with your all-time average, so improving and slipping are both obvious.

points.title: Your weakest area, one tap away
points.body: Once a case has enough answers to judge fairly, the lowest one is pinned to the home screen as a drill you can start straight away.

progress.availability: In the Android app. The browser version scores every answer but doesn't keep a profile yet.

panel.label: Skill profile
panel.caption: An illustration of the Stats screen, not real data.

meta.title: Download Bright for Android

download.title: Get Bright on Android
download.lede: Bright goes out as an APK on GitHub Releases. It's free, there's no account, and there's nothing to buy.
download.latestUnknown: The releases page has the newest build.

steps.title: Open the releases page on your phone
steps.body: Easiest if you download on the phone you're installing on. Take the .apk file attached to the newest release.

steps.title: Let Android install it
steps.body: It'll ask whether to allow installs from your browser or files app. That's a one-time thing, per app.

steps.title: Open it and pick a language
steps.body: You get a short intro, and Korean or English is chosen from your phone's language. Settings has it if you want to switch.

steps.title: Add a Groq key when it asks
steps.body: The AI runs on Groq's free tier. You can skip the key during setup — it only comes up again when a session actually needs it.

download.noPlayTitle: Why isn't it on Google Play?
download.noPlayBody: I tried submitting it once. Right now the time goes into the app instead of store review, so GitHub Releases is the real way to get it — and the app watches that same page to tell you when there's a new version.
download.iosBody: I'm porting it with Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform, so it shares a core with the Android app. There's no TestFlight build to hand out yet.

meta.title: Bright — frequently asked questions
meta.description: How Bright works, what it costs, where your history is stored, and what isn't built yet.

faq.title: Questions people ask
faq.lede: If something here is out of date or missing, open an issue on GitHub — that's the quickest way to reach me.

items.a: Nothing. There's no paid version, no subscription, no ads and no in-app purchases. The AI runs on Groq's free tier with a key you provide.

items.q: Do I really need a Groq key?
items.a: Yes, otherwise the AI can't answer. Getting one takes about a minute on Groq's site and the free tier is plenty for normal practice. You can skip it during setup, and the app only asks again when a session needs it.

items.q: Is it on the Play Store?
items.a: No. I tried submitting once, but I'm not chasing store distribution at the moment. The APK on GitHub Releases is how you install it.

items.q: Where do my sessions get saved?
items.a: In the app's own database on your phone. Nothing is uploaded, which also means it doesn't survive uninstalling and won't follow you to a new phone. Sign-in and sync are planned, not built.
No — the AI runs on a server, so a session needs a connection. Sessions you've already finished are readable offline.
Not yet. Voice input is something I want to add, but every release so far is typing only.
I'm working on it. It shares the same core as the Android app through Kotlin Multiplatform, but there's nothing to install yet.
Korean and English. It picks one from your phone's language on the first launch, and you can switch in settings whenever.

items.q: Can I trust what the AI tells me?
items.a: No, and please don't. It makes the cases up and it can be wrong while sounding certain. Treat the scoring and feedback as practice material, never as guidance for a real patient.
The releases repo is public; the source repo is private for now. That might change, but nothing about using the app depends on it.

items.q: How do I report a bug?
items.a: Open an issue on the public releases repo. It's a one-person project, so the honest answer on timing is whenever I get to it.

meta.title: Bright — privacy
meta.description: What Bright stores on your device, what leaves it, and what is never collected. No accounts, no analytics, no ads.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.lede: There's no account and no analytics, so almost everything stays on your phone. This page goes through exactly what happens to what you type.

sections.heading: The short version
bullets: Your sessions and history sit on your device and nowhere else.
What you type during a session goes to Groq, the AI provider, so it can write the reply. Nothing else leaves your phone while you're practising.
The app asks GitHub whether there's a newer release. That request carries nothing personal.
There's no account, no analytics or crash-reporting library, no ads and no third-party tracking in the app.
I never see your sessions. There's no server of mine for them to go to.

sections.heading: What's kept on your phone
paragraphs: The app keeps a local database on the device. It holds your practice sessions, the messages in them, and the per-question records that build your history and score summaries.
bullets: Sessions, messages and question records — the practice you've done.
Your language, the AI model you picked, and the flags that remember you've finished the intro.
Your Groq API key, in the app's own settings storage on the device.
A practice streak, and whether the app has already asked you about notifications.
sections.after: Uninstalling takes all of it with it. Since none of it is backed up anywhere, that's permanent — which is the trade-off for keeping everything local.

sections.heading: What leaves your phone
paragraphs: The app talks to two hosts and nothing else.
bullets: api.groq.com — while you're in a session, your messages and the case context go to Groq under your own API key so the AI can respond. What Groq does with that is covered by their privacy policy and the terms of the account your key belongs to.

api.github.com — the app reads the latest release of the public tyngzfgsf/Bright-app repository to tell you when an update is out. It's an ordinary anonymous request with no session content and no identifier attached.

sections.heading: What I never collect
bullets: No account, sign-in, email address or profile.
No analytics, telemetry or crash-reporting SDK is bundled in the app.
No advertising, and no advertising ID.
No contacts, location, photos or files from your phone.
Nothing sold or handed to data brokers, since there's nothing collected to sell.

sections.heading: Permissions the app asks for
bullets: Internet and network state — to reach the AI and check for updates.
Notifications — for practice reminders scheduled on the phone itself. There's no push server behind them.
Install packages — so the app can offer to install a newer release it downloaded from GitHub.
Microphone — declared for speech input. Where it's used the request goes to Android's own speech recognition rather than being recorded by the app, and no audio is stored.

sections.heading: This website
bullets: No analytics, no tracking pixels, no advertising cookies.
One cookie, NEXT_LOCALE, and only if you press the KO/EN switch, so your choice sticks. Automatic language detection never writes it.
Your light/dark preference lives in your browser's local storage and never leaves the browser.
The host keeps ordinary server request logs, like any web host does.

sections.heading: Please don't type real patient details
paragraphs: This is for practising on invented cases. Don't put real patients' details, identifiers or records in — that text would be sent to a third-party AI provider, and the app has nothing in it designed for handling real medical records.

sections.heading: What you can do about your data
bullets: Delete individual sessions from your history inside the app.
Remove or replace your Groq key in settings at any time.
Uninstall, and the local database and settings go with it.

sections.heading: Children
paragraphs: It's aimed at people training in emergency medicine, and isn't designed or directed at children.

sections.heading: What's coming
paragraphs: Sign-in and cloud sync are on the roadmap. Neither exists today, and neither will switch itself on quietly: when they ship they'll be something you choose in the app, and I'll rewrite this page before that release goes out.

sections.heading: Getting in touch
paragraphs: It's one person making this. Questions about privacy, or corrections to this page, are best raised as an issue on the public GitHub repository — that's also the fastest way to get an answer.

meta.title: Bright — terms of use
meta.description: The terms for using Bright, including the medical disclaimer: it is a training tool and not medical advice.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.lede: Plain terms for a free app made by one person. The first section is the one that matters: this is practice, not medical advice.

sections.heading: This isn't medical advice
paragraphs: Bright makes up emergency cases so you can practise responding to them. It's an educational tool. It isn't clinical decision support, it isn't a reference, and it doesn't stand in for training, supervision, protocols or your own judgement.
Don't use it to decide anything about a real patient. In a real emergency call your local emergency number — 119 in Korea, 911 in the US — or follow your institution's protocol.

sections.heading: The AI gets things wrong
paragraphs: The replies, cases, scores and feedback all come from a large language model. It can state something incorrect with complete confidence, misjudge a good answer, or invent details that don't match real practice or your local guidelines. Check anything you plan to rely on against a real source.

sections.heading: Using the app
bullets: It's free to use for your own training.
Don't enter real patient information, or anyone else's personal data, into a session.
Don't use it for anything unlawful, or in a way that breaks the terms of the AI provider whose key you're using.
Your API key is yours to look after, along with any usage charges on that account.

sections.heading: Other services involved
paragraphs: The AI runs on Groq using a key that belongs to you, so your use of it is governed by Groq's own terms and privacy policy. I have no control over their availability, pricing or how the models behave. Releases go out through GitHub, which has its own terms.

sections.heading: No warranty
paragraphs: The app is provided as is, with no warranty of any kind, express or implied, including fitness for a particular purpose. It's a free app built in spare time: it may have bugs, produce wrong output, lose data stored on your device, or stop working after a platform change.
As far as the law allows, I'm not liable for loss or damage arising from using the app or being unable to use it, including anything that comes from relying on its output.

sections.heading: It changes, and it might stop
paragraphs: This is still being built. Features can change or disappear, releases can be late, and the project could stop being maintained. Because releases are APKs on GitHub, a version you've already installed keeps working as long as your phone supports it.

sections.heading: Ownership
paragraphs: The app, its name and its design are mine. Downloading and using released builds is fine; redistributing modified copies as though they were Bright isn't. The sessions you write are yours.

sections.heading: Governing law
paragraphs: These terms follow the laws of the Republic of Korea, where I'm based, without regard to conflict-of-law rules.

sections.heading: If these terms change
paragraphs: The date at the top of the page changes with them. Carrying on using the app after that means the updated terms apply.

sections.heading: Getting in touch
paragraphs: Questions about any of this can go in an issue on the public GitHub repository.
